title: Government softens parts of cyber law draft, but 10-year rumour penalty stays
excerpt: Defamation penalties would fall to Penal Code levels and journalists gain new safeguards. Rights groups say the core problems remain.
content:
The government has revised its draft amendment to the country’s cyber law after consulting civil society, but the heaviest penalty in the draft, up to 10 years in prison for spreading rumours or misinformation, is unchanged, The Daily Star reported on 8 November.

The ICT Division first published the draft amendment for comment in mid-September. A cabinet committee led by Posts, Telecommunications and ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam has been reviewing it. Officials say 12 changes will be made, and the revised text will be published for further consultation before it is finalised.

What changes

  • Rumour: information would have to be false to count as a rumour. The September draft covered anything “unverified”.
  • Defamation: the penalty would match the Penal Code (up to two years, a fine or both), down from five years or Tk 20 lakh in the September draft.
  • Section 25: defamation, belittling and bullying would be separated from sextortion and sexual abuse offences.
  • Journalists: arresting journalists or media owners over their coverage would need a court’s approval, and outlets would get notice and a chance to respond.
  • Blocking content: authorities would have to give reasons within three days and decide appeals within 15 days. The “derogatory towards the state” ground for blocking would go.
  • Mobile courts would no longer try certain cyber offences.

What stays

The rumour and misinformation offence keeps its penalty of up to 10 years, a Tk 40 lakh fine or both. Powers to search, seize and arrest without a warrant under sections 33, 34 and 35 are not addressed.

Who said what

Dr Iftekharuzzaman, executive director of Transparency International Bangladesh, said the safeguards protect only journalists and media owners. “Such divide and rule should not be ideally acceptable to media professionals themselves,” he said, adding that speech and defamation belong in civil courts, not a cyber security law.

Sajjad Sharif, executive editor of Prothom Alo, welcomed the notice and time limits but said “the new draft should have also addressed sections 33, 34 and 35.” Supreme Court lawyer Priya Ahsan Chowdhury said rumour should not remain an offence at all.

Why it matters

NGOs, researchers and rights defenders publish reports, survey findings and social media posts that officials may dispute. A broadly worded rumour offence with a 10-year penalty, and warrantless search powers, carry real risk for civil society, not only for the press. The extra safeguards cover journalists and media outlets, not NGO staff or citizens.

What to watch

Publication of the revised text, the length of the next consultation, and whether NGO networks submit joint comments before the bill goes to the cabinet and Parliament.
